filters.description:
NetObserv filter expression passed to the console plugin (plain text; the client URL-encodes it).

Syntax:
- key=value — exact match; key=a,b — OR multiple values for the same key
- key~pattern — regex / contains match; key!~pattern — NOT regex
- key!=value — not equal; key>number — numeric greater-or-equal (e.g. Bytes>1000)
- AND within a group: & (e.g. SrcK8S_Namespace=default&Proto=6)
- OR between groups: | (e.g. SrcK8S_Name=pod-a|SrcK8S_Name=pod-b)

Prefer the dedicated "namespace" parameter for namespace scope when possible.
Use Kubernetes list tools (namespaces, pods, deployments, etc.) to discover filter values.

Common Kubernetes fields (Src/Dst prefixes mirror each other):
- SrcK8S_Namespace, DstK8S_Namespace, SrcK8S_Name, DstK8S_Name
- SrcK8S_Type, DstK8S_Type (e.g. Pod, Service, Node)
- SrcK8S_OwnerName, DstK8S_OwnerName, SrcK8S_OwnerType, DstK8S_OwnerType (for Deployment, StatefulSet, etc.)
- SrcK8S_HostName, DstK8S_HostName, SrcK8S_Zone, DstK8S_Zone, K8S_ClusterName, UDN

Network & flow:
- SrcAddr, DstAddr (IPs), SrcPort, DstPort, Proto (IANA number, e.g. 6=TCP, 17=UDP)
- FlowDirection (0=Ingress, 1=Egress, 2=Inner), Bytes, Packets, Dscp, Flags

Packet drops (often with recordType flowLog and packetLoss dropped/hasDrops):
- PktDropPackets, PktDropBytes, PktDropLatestState, PktDropLatestDropCause

DNS:
- DnsName, DnsId, DnsLatencyMs, DnsErrno, DnsFlagsResponseCode

Examples:
- SrcK8S_Namespace=openshift-netobserv&SrcK8S_Name~my-app
- Proto=6&DstPort=443
- SrcK8S_Name=pod-a|SrcK8S_Name=pod-b

tools.name: netobserv_get_flow_metrics
tools.description: Returns aggregated NetObserv flow metrics as topology or time-series data. Use for throughput, TLS/DNS/drop breakdowns, and namespace or workload traffic analysis; see aggregateBy and groups for grouping options.

aggregateBy.description:
Primary dimension for netobserv_get_flow_metrics (console plugin /api/flow/metrics).

Two forms (use exact spelling):

1) Topology scopes — aggregate endpoints for graph/topology views:
- app — application workloads (pods/services), excluding infrastructure traffic
- namespace — Kubernetes namespace (default)
- owner — controller owner (Deployment, StatefulSet, …)
- resource — pod, service, or node (finest workload granularity)
- host — node name
- zone — availability zone
- cluster — cluster name (multi-cluster)
- network — user-defined / secondary network name

2) Flow record fields — group by a single flow attribute (PascalCase field name).
Use for breakdown charts (TLS, DNS, drops, protocol). Field names match filters / flow logs.

TLS (requires TLS tracking on the FlowCollector):
- TLSVersion, TLSCipherSuite, TLSGroup, TLSTypes

DNS:
- DnsName, DnsFlagsResponseCode, DnsErrno

Packet drops:
- PktDropLatestState, PktDropLatestDropCause

Network / K8s (single-sided breakdown; pair with filters for src/dst):
- Proto, SrcPort, DstPort, FlowDirection, Dscp
- SrcK8S_Namespace, DstK8S_Namespace, SrcK8S_Name, DstK8S_Name
- SrcK8S_Type, DstK8S_Type, SrcK8S_OwnerName, DstK8S_OwnerName
- SrcK8S_HostName, DstK8S_HostName, SrcK8S_Zone, DstK8S_Zone
- K8S_ClusterName, SrcK8S_NetworkName, DstK8S_NetworkName

Pair aggregateBy with type and function:
- Throughput: type=Bytes or Packets, function=rate
- Flow count: type=Flows, function=count or rate
- DNS volume: type=DnsFlows, function=count
- DNS latency: type=DnsLatencyMs, function=avg, p90, or max
- RTT: type=TimeFlowRttNs, function=avg, min, or p90
- Drops: type=PktDropPackets or PktDropBytes, function=rate

Examples:
- aggregateBy=namespace, type=Bytes, function=rate
- aggregateBy=TLSVersion, type=Bytes, function=rate, filters=TLSTypes!~""
- aggregateBy=TLSGroup, type=Flows, function=count
- aggregateBy=DnsFlagsResponseCode, type=DnsFlows, function=count
- aggregateBy=PktDropLatestState, type=PktDropPackets, function=rate, packetLoss=dropped
- aggregateBy=resource, type=Bytes, function=rate, namespace=netobserv

Done.

What I applied
- Canary Deployment
  - Name: engine-v2-1 (namespace: canary-deployment-ns)
  - Replicas: 2
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - Container: rec-engine
    - Port: 80/TCP (matches stable)
    - Security: same as stable (no additional securityContext)

- Service update
  - Service: recommendation-engine (namespace: canary-deployment-ns)
  - Selector changed from app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0 to app=recommendation-engine
  - Now targets both engine-v2-0 and engine-v2-1, yielding ~50/50 traffic with equal pod counts
  - Port: 80, targetPort: 8080 (unchanged, same as before)

Current state
- Stable pods (v2.0): 2 Running
- Canary pods (v2.1): 2 Running
- Service selector: app=recommendation-engine (matches both versions)

How to verify
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get pods -l app=recommendation-engine -o wide
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get endpoints recommendation-engine
  - You should see 4 endpoints (2 from v2.0, 2 from v2.1)
- Optional: curl the service repeatedly and observe backend pod IPs to see ~50/50 distribution

Rollback/adjustment tips
- To stop canary quickly: scale engine-v2-1 to 0 replicas
- To shift weight: adjust replicas on engine-v2-0 and engine-v2-1 proportionally (e.g., 3 vs 1 for ~75/25) or use an ingress/service mesh for precise weights if needed.

outputSteps.content:
Done. I created NetworkPolicy np in namespace ns1.

Behavior:
- Egress allowed to any pod in namespace ns2 (any port)
- Egress allowed on DNS ports 53/TCP and 53/UDP to any destination
- All other egress is denied
- Ingress is unaffected

If you want DNS to be allowed only to the cluster DNS (e.g., kube-system/coredns), I can update the policy to target that specifically instead of allowing port 53 to all destinations.

results.taskOutput:
I fixed it. Here’s what I did and the current state:

- Root cause: The pod was Pending because its PVC homepage-pvc was Pending. The PVC referenced a non-existent StorageClass named sc. Scheduler event: “pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims.”
- Fix applied: Created a StorageClass named sc using the same provisioner as your cluster’s default (k8s.io/minikube-hostpath). This allowed dynamic provisioning to bind the PVC.
- Current state:
  - PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi, RWO)
  - Pod homepage-pod: Running, Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster (container nginx started and ready)

If you’d prefer to use an existing StorageClass (e.g., standard or csi-hostpath-sc) instead of the new sc, I can:
- Repoint the PVC to the desired StorageClass and re-provision, or
- Delete the sc StorageClass after migration.

Want me to switch the PVC to one of your existing StorageClasses, or keep it as-is?

namespace/homepage-ns created
persistentvolumeclaim/homepage-pvc created
pod/homepage-pod created

I fixed it. Here’s what I did and the current state:

- Root cause: The pod was Pending because its PVC homepage-pvc was Pending. The PVC referenced a non-existent StorageClass named sc. Scheduler event: “pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims.”
- Fix applied: Created a StorageClass named sc using the same provisioner as your cluster’s default (k8s.io/minikube-hostpath). This allowed dynamic provisioning to bind the PVC.
- Current state:
  - PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi, RWO)
  - Pod homepage-pod: Running, Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster (container nginx started and ready)

If you’d prefer to use an existing StorageClass (e.g., standard or csi-hostpath-sc) instead of the new sc, I can:
- Repoint the PVC to the desired StorageClass and re-provision, or
- Delete the sc StorageClass after migration.

Want me to switch the PVC to one of your existing StorageClasses, or keep it as-is?

outputSteps.content:
I fixed it. Here’s what I did and the current state:

- Root cause: The pod was Pending because its PVC homepage-pvc was Pending. The PVC referenced a non-existent StorageClass named sc. Scheduler event: “pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims.”
- Fix applied: Created a StorageClass named sc using the same provisioner as your cluster’s default (k8s.io/minikube-hostpath). This allowed dynamic provisioning to bind the PVC.
- Current state:
  - PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi, RWO)
  - Pod homepage-pod: Running, Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster (container nginx started and ready)

If you’d prefer to use an existing StorageClass (e.g., standard or csi-hostpath-sc) instead of the new sc, I can:
- Repoint the PVC to the desired StorageClass and re-provision, or
- Delete the sc StorageClass after migration.

Want me to switch the PVC to one of your existing StorageClasses, or keep it as-is?

results.taskOutput:
I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The pod was Running but failing readiness/liveness probes. Events showed connection refused on http://<pod-ip>:80/get_status and /is_ready.
- The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080 (not 80), and those custom probe paths don’t exist on stock nginx.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment in orders/webapp:
  - Probes now GET / on port 8080.
  - Exposed container port 8080 (named http).
- Updated the Service orders/webapp to target the named port http (8080).

Current status
- Deployment: 1/1 available.
- Pod: webapp-7f66647687-qwpzf is Ready (1/1).
- Endpoints: service points to 10.244.0.25:8080.

How to verify
- In-cluster: curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local
- From a pod: kubectl -n orders run -it tmp --rm --image=registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/ubi-minimal -- curl -sS http://webapp

Need external access? There’s no Ingress/Route configured. If you want it public, tell me your hostname/path and I’ll create an Ingress (or OpenShift Route).

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: webapp
  namespace: orders
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: webapp
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 25%
      maxUnavailable: 25%
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: webapp
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: webapp
          image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest
          imagePullPolicy: Always
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
              name: http
              protocol: TCP
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: 8080
              scheme: HTTP
            initialDelaySeconds: 2
            periodSeconds: 5
            timeoutSeconds: 2
            failureThreshold: 3
            successThreshold: 1
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: 8080
              scheme: HTTP
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 10
            timeoutSeconds: 2
            failureThreshold: 3
            successThreshold: 1
          resources: {}
      dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
      restartPolicy: Always
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30

outputSteps.content:
I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The pod was Running but failing readiness/liveness probes. Events showed connection refused on http://<pod-ip>:80/get_status and /is_ready.
- The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080 (not 80), and those custom probe paths don’t exist on stock nginx.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment in orders/webapp:
  - Probes now GET / on port 8080.
  - Exposed container port 8080 (named http).
- Updated the Service orders/webapp to target the named port http (8080).

Current status
- Deployment: 1/1 available.
- Pod: webapp-7f66647687-qwpzf is Ready (1/1).
- Endpoints: service points to 10.244.0.25:8080.

How to verify
- In-cluster: curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local
- From a pod: kubectl -n orders run -it tmp --rm --image=registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/ubi-minimal -- curl -sS http://webapp

Need external access? There’s no Ingress/Route configured. If you want it public, tell me your hostname/path and I’ll create an Ingress (or OpenShift Route).

Steps.message:
Checking if the pod is running and ready...
pod/webapp-7f66647687-qwpzf condition met
Success: Pod is now Ready
Current liveness probe path: /
Current readiness probe path: /
Success: Both probe paths have been fixed
Success: Pod is stable with acceptable number of restarts

results.taskOutput:
Root cause
- The Role bound to your pod-reader service account only allowed listing apps/deployments. It did not grant any permissions on core/pods, so listing pods was denied.

What I changed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include permissions on pods in the core API group:
  - resources: pods
  - verbs: get, list, watch
- Kept the existing apps/deployments list permission.

This fixes pod listing for the pod-reader service account in the simple-rbac-setup namespace.

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i list pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader
  Expected: yes
- Or:
  kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

If you also want describe/logs/exec, I can add get/watch on events and get/watch on pods/logs or broader verbs as needed.

Diagnosis
- Root cause: The Service selector didn’t match your Pods.
  - Service nginx (web) was selecting app=web.
  - Deployment/Pods are labeled app=nginx.
  - Result: the Service had no endpoints, so connections to it failed.

What I changed
- Updated the Service selector to app=nginx so it matches the Deployment’s Pods.
- Verified endpoints are now populated (10.244.0.26:8080).
- Launched a short-lived curl pod and confirmed:
  - DNS resolves: nginx.web.svc.cluster.local -> 10.101.133.165
  - curl to nginx:80 succeeded (Service is reachable inside the cluster).

Current status
- nginx Service works for in-cluster clients on port 80.
- No NetworkPolicies or Ingress are present; Service type is ClusterIP, so it is not reachable from outside the cluster (by design).

If you need external access, pick one and I can set it up:
- Ingress: front the Service on a hostname (requires an Ingress controller and DNS).
- NodePort: expose on each node’s IP at a high port.
- LoadBalancer: get a cloud/external LB IP (if supported by your environment).

Let me know which exposure method you prefer, and I’ll create it. I can also remove the test pod (curl-tester) if you’d like.

Steps.message:
namespace/web created
deployment.apps/nginx created
service/nginx created

Diagnosis
- Root cause: The Service selector didn’t match your Pods.
  - Service nginx (web) was selecting app=web.
  - Deployment/Pods are labeled app=nginx.
  - Result: the Service had no endpoints, so connections to it failed.

What I changed
- Updated the Service selector to app=nginx so it matches the Deployment’s Pods.
- Verified endpoints are now populated (10.244.0.26:8080).
- Launched a short-lived curl pod and confirmed:
  - DNS resolves: nginx.web.svc.cluster.local -> 10.101.133.165
  - curl to nginx:80 succeeded (Service is reachable inside the cluster).

Current status
- nginx Service works for in-cluster clients on port 80.
- No NetworkPolicies or Ingress are present; Service type is ClusterIP, so it is not reachable from outside the cluster (by design).

If you need external access, pick one and I can set it up:
- Ingress: front the Service on a hostname (requires an Ingress controller and DNS).
- NodePort: expose on each node’s IP at a high port.
- LoadBalancer: get a cloud/external LB IP (if supported by your environment).

Let me know which exposure method you prefer, and I’ll create it. I can also remove the test pod (curl-tester) if you’d like.

Diagnosis
- Root cause: The Service selector didn’t match your Pods.
  - Service nginx (web) was selecting app=web.
  - Deployment/Pods are labeled app=nginx.
  - Result: the Service had no endpoints, so connections to it failed.

What I changed
- Updated the Service selector to app=nginx so it matches the Deployment’s Pods.
- Verified endpoints are now populated (10.244.0.26:8080).
- Launched a short-lived curl pod and confirmed:
  - DNS resolves: nginx.web.svc.cluster.local -> 10.101.133.165
  - curl to nginx:80 succeeded (Service is reachable inside the cluster).

Current status
- nginx Service works for in-cluster clients on port 80.
- No NetworkPolicies or Ingress are present; Service type is ClusterIP, so it is not reachable from outside the cluster (by design).

If you need external access, pick one and I can set it up:
- Ingress: front the Service on a hostname (requires an Ingress controller and DNS).
- NodePort: expose on each node’s IP at a high port.
- LoadBalancer: get a cloud/external LB IP (if supported by your environment).

Let me know which exposure method you prefer, and I’ll create it. I can also remove the test pod (curl-tester) if you’d like.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- Root cause: The web-app pods were stuck Pending due to a nodeSelector constraint that doesn’t match any node.
  - Deployment had spec.template.spec.nodeSelector: environment: production-gpu
  - Scheduler events: “0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.”
  - The only node (mcp-eval-cluster) doesn’t have label environment=production-gpu.
- Because no pods were scheduled, the Service had no endpoints, so connections to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 returned “connection refused.”

What I changed
- Removed the incompatible nodeSelector by recreating the Deployment without it.
  - Deleted Deployment webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment.
  - Recreated Deployment with replicas: 2 and no nodeSelector.

Current state (verified)
- Pods: 2/2 Running
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-7h2n7 (10.244.0.31)
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-w6j5p (10.244.0.30)
- Service endpoints: present
  - EndpointSlice web-app-service-h2jj7 ports: 80, endpoints: 10.244.0.31,10.244.0.30

Why this fixes the issue
- With pods now running and selected by app=web-app, kube-proxy programs endpoints for the Service. Traffic to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 should now succeed.

Optional validation you can run
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend run tmp --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 -- wget -qO- http://web-app-service
  Expect an nginx welcome page (200 OK).

If you intended to restrict to GPU nodes
- Either label the intended node(s) with environment=production-gpu, or
- Adjust the Deployment’s nodeSelector/affinity to match actual node labels, and ensure such nodes exist and are schedulable.

Would you like me to:
- Pin the image tag (avoid latest),
- Add readiness/liveness probes,
- Reinstate a corrected nodeSelector/affinity,
- Or run an in-cluster curl to confirm end-to-end?

Steps.message:
namespace/webshop-frontend created
service/web-app-service created
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment created
Waiting for resources to be created...
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment condition met
Warning: v1 Endpoints is deprecated in v1.33+; use discovery.k8s.io/v1 EndpointSlice
Setup successful: Service has no endpoints as expected

Diagnosis
- Root cause: The web-app pods were stuck Pending due to a nodeSelector constraint that doesn’t match any node.
  - Deployment had spec.template.spec.nodeSelector: environment: production-gpu
  - Scheduler events: “0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.”
  - The only node (mcp-eval-cluster) doesn’t have label environment=production-gpu.
- Because no pods were scheduled, the Service had no endpoints, so connections to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 returned “connection refused.”

What I changed
- Removed the incompatible nodeSelector by recreating the Deployment without it.
  - Deleted Deployment webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment.
  - Recreated Deployment with replicas: 2 and no nodeSelector.

Current state (verified)
- Pods: 2/2 Running
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-7h2n7 (10.244.0.31)
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-w6j5p (10.244.0.30)
- Service endpoints: present
  - EndpointSlice web-app-service-h2jj7 ports: 80, endpoints: 10.244.0.31,10.244.0.30

Why this fixes the issue
- With pods now running and selected by app=web-app, kube-proxy programs endpoints for the Service. Traffic to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 should now succeed.

Optional validation you can run
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend run tmp --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 -- wget -qO- http://web-app-service
  Expect an nginx welcome page (200 OK).

If you intended to restrict to GPU nodes
- Either label the intended node(s) with environment=production-gpu, or
- Adjust the Deployment’s nodeSelector/affinity to match actual node labels, and ensure such nodes exist and are schedulable.

Would you like me to:
- Pin the image tag (avoid latest),
- Add readiness/liveness probes,
- Reinstate a corrected nodeSelector/affinity,
- Or run an in-cluster curl to confirm end-to-end?

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- Root cause: The web-app pods were stuck Pending due to a nodeSelector constraint that doesn’t match any node.
  - Deployment had spec.template.spec.nodeSelector: environment: production-gpu
  - Scheduler events: “0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.”
  - The only node (mcp-eval-cluster) doesn’t have label environment=production-gpu.
- Because no pods were scheduled, the Service had no endpoints, so connections to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 returned “connection refused.”

What I changed
- Removed the incompatible nodeSelector by recreating the Deployment without it.
  - Deleted Deployment webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment.
  - Recreated Deployment with replicas: 2 and no nodeSelector.

Current state (verified)
- Pods: 2/2 Running
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-7h2n7 (10.244.0.31)
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-w6j5p (10.244.0.30)
- Service endpoints: present
  - EndpointSlice web-app-service-h2jj7 ports: 80, endpoints: 10.244.0.31,10.244.0.30

Why this fixes the issue
- With pods now running and selected by app=web-app, kube-proxy programs endpoints for the Service. Traffic to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 should now succeed.

Optional validation you can run
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend run tmp --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 -- wget -qO- http://web-app-service
  Expect an nginx welcome page (200 OK).

If you intended to restrict to GPU nodes
- Either label the intended node(s) with environment=production-gpu, or
- Adjust the Deployment’s nodeSelector/affinity to match actual node labels, and ensure such nodes exist and are schedulable.

Would you like me to:
- Pin the image tag (avoid latest),
- Add readiness/liveness probes,
- Reinstate a corrected nodeSelector/affinity,
- Or run an in-cluster curl to confirm end-to-end?

I’ve set up the requested multi-tenant development environment. Summary of what’s been created and enforced:

1) Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labels used for policy scoping:
  - dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: env=dev
  - dev-shared: env=shared
  - staging: env=staging
  - prod: env=prod

2) RBAC
- ServiceAccounts:
  - dev-alice/alice-sa
  - dev-bob/bob-sa
  - dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Per-developer full access to their own namespace:
  - RoleBinding in each dev namespace binding the developer User and their SA to ClusterRole edit (broad namespace-level control without RBAC admin rights).
- Read-only to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared granting view to Users alice, bob, charlie and to SAs alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie).
- Staging/prod:
  - No developer bindings were created; only cluster-admins (via existing clusterrolebinding) can access.

3) ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie (rq-standard):
  - requests.cpu=2, limits.cpu=2
  - requests.memory=4Gi, limits.memory=4Gi
  - pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared (rq-shared):
  - requests.cpu=4, limits.cpu=4
  - requests.memory=8Gi, limits.memory=8Gi
  - pods=20, services=10
- staging (rq-staging) and prod (rq-prod):
  - requests.cpu=8, limits.cpu=8
  - requests.memory=16Gi, limits.memory=16Gi
  - pods=50, services=20

4) NetworkPolicies and isolation
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in all 6 namespaces.
- Allow DNS egress from all 6 namespaces to kube-dns/CoreDNS in kube-system on TCP/UDP 53.
- Same-namespace allow (Ingress and Egress) in each namespace.
- Dev-to-shared access only:
  - In dev namespaces: allow Ingress/Egress to/from dev-shared.
  - In dev-shared: allow Ingress/Egress to/from namespaces labeled env=dev.
- Cross-developer blocked:
  - No policies allow traffic between dev namespaces; default deny plus same-namespace-only ensures isolation.
- Staging/prod isolation:
  - Only same-namespace traffic and DNS egress allowed; no allowances to dev or dev-shared, providing complete isolation from dev.

5) Default deny everywhere except system
- Applied default-deny in the created app namespaces (dev-*, dev-shared, staging, prod). System namespaces (e.g., kube-system) were not modified.

Notes and validation
- If your DNS runs outside kube-system or uses different labels (e.g., CoreDNS with app.kubernetes.io/name=coredns or OpenShift’s openshift-dns), update the allow-dns-egress policies accordingly.
- To validate:
  - kubectl get ns
  - kubectl -n dev-alice get sa,rolebinding,resourcequota
  - kubectl -n dev-shared get rolebinding,resourcequota
  - kubectl -n dev-alice get networkpolicy (repeat for other namespaces)
- ServiceAccount tokens (on Kubernetes v1.24+): kubectl -n dev-alice create token alice-sa (repeat for others) if you need short-lived tokens.

This configuration follows least-privilege principles: developers get edit rights only in their own namespaces, view in shared, no dev access to staging/prod; network policies strictly contain traffic to same-namespace and dev-shared, with DNS egress permitted.

Steps.message:
Setting up cluster state for dev environment eval...
Setup completed successfully

I’ve set up the requested multi-tenant development environment. Summary of what’s been created and enforced:

1) Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labels used for policy scoping:
  - dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: env=dev
  - dev-shared: env=shared
  - staging: env=staging
  - prod: env=prod

2) RBAC
- ServiceAccounts:
  - dev-alice/alice-sa
  - dev-bob/bob-sa
  - dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Per-developer full access to their own namespace:
  - RoleBinding in each dev namespace binding the developer User and their SA to ClusterRole edit (broad namespace-level control without RBAC admin rights).
- Read-only to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared granting view to Users alice, bob, charlie and to SAs alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie).
- Staging/prod:
  - No developer bindings were created; only cluster-admins (via existing clusterrolebinding) can access.

3) ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie (rq-standard):
  - requests.cpu=2, limits.cpu=2
  - requests.memory=4Gi, limits.memory=4Gi
  - pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared (rq-shared):
  - requests.cpu=4, limits.cpu=4
  - requests.memory=8Gi, limits.memory=8Gi
  - pods=20, services=10
- staging (rq-staging) and prod (rq-prod):
  - requests.cpu=8, limits.cpu=8
  - requests.memory=16Gi, limits.memory=16Gi
  - pods=50, services=20

4) NetworkPolicies and isolation
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in all 6 namespaces.
- Allow DNS egress from all 6 namespaces to kube-dns/CoreDNS in kube-system on TCP/UDP 53.
- Same-namespace allow (Ingress and Egress) in each namespace.
- Dev-to-shared access only:
  - In dev namespaces: allow Ingress/Egress to/from dev-shared.
  - In dev-shared: allow Ingress/Egress to/from namespaces labeled env=dev.
- Cross-developer blocked:
  - No policies allow traffic between dev namespaces; default deny plus same-namespace-only ensures isolation.
- Staging/prod isolation:
  - Only same-namespace traffic and DNS egress allowed; no allowances to dev or dev-shared, providing complete isolation from dev.

5) Default deny everywhere except system
- Applied default-deny in the created app namespaces (dev-*, dev-shared, staging, prod). System namespaces (e.g., kube-system) were not modified.

Notes and validation
- If your DNS runs outside kube-system or uses different labels (e.g., CoreDNS with app.kubernetes.io/name=coredns or OpenShift’s openshift-dns), update the allow-dns-egress policies accordingly.
- To validate:
  - kubectl get ns
  - kubectl -n dev-alice get sa,rolebinding,resourcequota
  - kubectl -n dev-shared get rolebinding,resourcequota
  - kubectl -n dev-alice get networkpolicy (repeat for other namespaces)
- ServiceAccount tokens (on Kubernetes v1.24+): kubectl -n dev-alice create token alice-sa (repeat for others) if you need short-lived tokens.

This configuration follows least-privilege principles: developers get edit rights only in their own namespaces, view in shared, no dev access to staging/prod; network policies strictly contain traffic to same-namespace and dev-shared, with DNS egress permitted.

outputSteps.content:
I’ve set up the requested multi-tenant development environment. Summary of what’s been created and enforced:

1) Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labels used for policy scoping:
  - dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: env=dev
  - dev-shared: env=shared
  - staging: env=staging
  - prod: env=prod

2) RBAC
- ServiceAccounts:
  - dev-alice/alice-sa
  - dev-bob/bob-sa
  - dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Per-developer full access to their own namespace:
  - RoleBinding in each dev namespace binding the developer User and their SA to ClusterRole edit (broad namespace-level control without RBAC admin rights).
- Read-only to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared granting view to Users alice, bob, charlie and to SAs alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie).
- Staging/prod:
  - No developer bindings were created; only cluster-admins (via existing clusterrolebinding) can access.

3) ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie (rq-standard):
  - requests.cpu=2, limits.cpu=2
  - requests.memory=4Gi, limits.memory=4Gi
  - pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared (rq-shared):
  - requests.cpu=4, limits.cpu=4
  - requests.memory=8Gi, limits.memory=8Gi
  - pods=20, services=10
- staging (rq-staging) and prod (rq-prod):
  - requests.cpu=8, limits.cpu=8
  - requests.memory=16Gi, limits.memory=16Gi
  - pods=50, services=20

4) NetworkPolicies and isolation
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in all 6 namespaces.
- Allow DNS egress from all 6 namespaces to kube-dns/CoreDNS in kube-system on TCP/UDP 53.
- Same-namespace allow (Ingress and Egress) in each namespace.
- Dev-to-shared access only:
  - In dev namespaces: allow Ingress/Egress to/from dev-shared.
  - In dev-shared: allow Ingress/Egress to/from namespaces labeled env=dev.
- Cross-developer blocked:
  - No policies allow traffic between dev namespaces; default deny plus same-namespace-only ensures isolation.
- Staging/prod isolation:
  - Only same-namespace traffic and DNS egress allowed; no allowances to dev or dev-shared, providing complete isolation from dev.

5) Default deny everywhere except system
- Applied default-deny in the created app namespaces (dev-*, dev-shared, staging, prod). System namespaces (e.g., kube-system) were not modified.

Notes and validation
- If your DNS runs outside kube-system or uses different labels (e.g., CoreDNS with app.kubernetes.io/name=coredns or OpenShift’s openshift-dns), update the allow-dns-egress policies accordingly.
- To validate:
  - kubectl get ns
  - kubectl -n dev-alice get sa,rolebinding,resourcequota
  - kubectl -n dev-shared get rolebinding,resourcequota
  - kubectl -n dev-alice get networkpolicy (repeat for other namespaces)
- ServiceAccount tokens (on Kubernetes v1.24+): kubectl -n dev-alice create token alice-sa (repeat for others) if you need short-lived tokens.

This configuration follows least-privilege principles: developers get edit rights only in their own namespaces, view in shared, no dev access to staging/prod; network policies strictly contain traffic to same-namespace and dev-shared, with DNS egress permitted.

Done.

What I set up
- Namespace: statefulset-test
- Headless Service: db (clusterIP=None) to back the StatefulSet

- PVCs for db-1 and db-2 are retained (so their data is preserved).

- kubectl -n statefulset-test exec db-0 -- sh -c "cat /data/test"
